### Questions

`meta` has one row per author, with columns such as `era` and `gender`. `text_en`
has the text of each author's English Wikipedia page, and `text_fr` has the text of
the French page. This is the corpus the chapter uses.

Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save
it to a variable.

1. Using `meta`, count the number of authors in each `era`.

```{python}
(
    meta
    .group_by(c.era)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
)
```

2. Using `text_en`, add a column `n_chars` with the number of characters in each
page, using `c.text.str.len_chars()`. Select `doc_id` and `n_chars` and sort from
the longest to the shortest page.

```{python}
(
    text_en
    .with_columns(n_chars = c.text.str.len_chars())
    .select(c.doc_id, c.n_chars)
    .sort(c.n_chars, descending=True)
)
```

3. `text_en` has 75 rows, but `text_fr` has only 73. Find the authors that have no
French page by anti-joining `text_en` to `text_fr.select(c.doc_id)` with
`how="anti"`.

```{python}
(
    text_en
    .join(text_fr.select(c.doc_id), on=c.doc_id, how="anti")
)
```

The two authors are Rex Warner and Edward Upward. Question 2 showed that they have
the shortest and the third-shortest English pages.

4. The block below is given. It runs each language's text through its own spaCy
model, as in the chapter, and saves the results as `anno_en` and `anno_fr`. It takes
a few minutes to run.

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
anno_en = DSText.process(text_en, nlp_en)
anno_fr = DSText.process(text_fr, nlp_fr)
anno_fr
```

5. Using `anno_fr`, count the number of tokens with each part of speech (`upos`).
Sort from most to least common.

```{python}
(
    anno_fr
    .group_by(c.upos)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

6. Stack the two annotation tables with a `lang` column, as in the chapter:

```python
pl.concat([
    anno_en.with_columns(lang = pl.lit("en")),
    anno_fr.with_columns(lang = pl.lit("fr"))
])
```

Then count the tokens for each `lang` and `upos`, add a column
`prop = c.count / c.count.sum().over(c.lang)`, and keep only the rows where `upos`
is `"DET"`.

```{python}
(
    pl.concat([
        anno_en.with_columns(lang = pl.lit("en")),
        anno_fr.with_columns(lang = pl.lit("fr"))
    ])
    .group_by(c.lang, c.upos)
    .agg(count = pl.len())
    .with_columns(prop = c.count / c.count.sum().over(c.lang))
    .filter(c.upos == "DET")
)
```

8.9% of the English tokens are determiners, against 12.2% of the French tokens.
Nearly every French noun needs an article in front of it.

7. Take the code from the previous question without the last filter. Draw a bar
plot with `upos` on the x-axis and `prop` on the y-axis, using
`.geom_col(aes(fill=c.lang), position="dodge")` and `coord_flip()`.

```{python}
(
    pl.concat([
        anno_en.with_columns(lang = pl.lit("en")),
        anno_fr.with_columns(lang = pl.lit("fr"))
    ])
    .group_by(c.lang, c.upos)
    .agg(count = pl.len())
    .with_columns(prop = c.count / c.count.sum().over(c.lang))
    .ggplot(aes(c.upos, c.prop))
    .geom_col(aes(fill=c.lang), position="dodge")
    .coord_flip()
)
```

French also has a larger share of nouns and prepositions (`ADP`), while English has
more proper nouns (`PROPN`). These differences come from the grammar of the two
languages, not from what the pages say about the authors.

8. Compute the TF-IDF scores for `anno_en` with `min_df=0.01` and `max_df=0.5`.
Keep only the authors `"Jane Austen"`, `"A. A. Milne"`, and `"T. S. Eliot"` using
`c.doc_id.is_in(...)`, and then find the top 10 terms for each author, joined into a
single string, as in the chapter.

```{python}
(
    DSText.compute_tfidf(anno_en, min_df=0.01, max_df=0.5)
    .filter(c.doc_id.is_in(["Jane Austen", "A. A. Milne", "T. S. Eliot"]))
    .sort([c.doc_id, c.tfidf], descending=[False, True])
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .head(10)
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(top_lemmas = c.lemma.str.join("; "))
)
```

The lists pick out what each author is known for: Pooh and Christopher Robin for
Milne, The Waste Land and Prufrock for Eliot, and the novels for Austen. But the
word `parser` shows up for both Milne and Eliot, and `output` for Eliot.

9. Do the same as the previous question, but for `anno_fr`.

```{python}
(
    DSText.compute_tfidf(anno_fr, min_df=0.01, max_df=0.5)
    .filter(c.doc_id.is_in(["Jane Austen", "A. A. Milne", "T. S. Eliot"]))
    .sort([c.doc_id, c.tfidf], descending=[False, True])
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .head(10)
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(top_lemmas = c.lemma.str.join("; "))
)
```

The French lists find some of the same names and titles, such as Prufrock and
Mansfield Park, but they are noisier, with words like `je`, `quel`, and `with`.
Milne's French list does not mention Pooh at all.

10. Using `text_en`, add a column `n` that counts how many times the string
`"mw-parser-output"` appears in each page, using
`c.text.str.count_matches("mw-parser-output")`. Keep the rows where `n` is greater
than zero and select `doc_id` and `n`.

```{python}
(
    text_en
    .with_columns(n = c.text.str.count_matches("mw-parser-output"))
    .filter(c.n > 0)
    .select(c.doc_id, c.n)
)
```

`"mw-parser-output"` is leftover code from the Wikipedia web page that ended up in
the text. It appears 22 times in Eliot's page and 8 times in Milne's, which is why
`parser` made their lists in question 8. spaCy treats `parser` as an ordinary word,
so filtering on `is_alpha` does not remove it.

11. Build a 2D UMAP projection of the French pages, as in the chapter, with
`min_df=0.01`, `max_df=0.5`, and `random_state=42`. Join the result to
`meta.select(c.doc_id, c.short, c.era)` and plot the `short` names with
`geom_text`, colored by `era`.

```{python}
(
    anno_fr
    .pipe(
        umap_text,
        doc_id=c.doc_id,
        term_id=c.lemma,
        n_components=2,
        min_df=0.01,
        max_df=0.5,
        random_state=42
    )
    .predict(full=True)
    .join(meta.select(c.doc_id, c.short, c.era), on=c.doc_id)
    .ggplot(aes(c.dr0, c.dr1))
    .geom_text(aes(label=c.short, color=c.era), size=6)
)
```

The colors are mixed across the whole plot, and no region belongs to a single era.
Authors end up near each other when their pages share names and places, not
because they wrote in the same century.
